description: Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Chrome OS, Linux and Unix — how each OS shapes HCI design decisions.
hero_keywords: multiple device screens laptop smartphone tablet
hero_image_caption: A range of devices showing different operating system interfaces side by side.
content_html:
What Does an Operating System Do?

Before you can design or use an HCI, something must manage the hardware, run the software and provide the interface layer between the user and the machine. That something is the operating system (OS). Every digital device — from a smartphone in your pocket to a server in a data centre — runs an operating system. The OS performs three core jobs: it manages hardware resources (telling the processor, RAM and storage when and how to be used), it runs software applications, and it presents the HCI through which users interact with the device.

This topic is flagged by examiners as content that is not covered in the coursework units — which means students who revise only from their NEA projects often miss it entirely. The exam asks you to name specific operating systems, describe their key characteristics and explain how the OS choice shapes the HCI design.

Desktop and Laptop Operating Systems

Windows is the dominant desktop OS in most business and educational environments. Its HCI is built around a taskbar at the bottom of the screen, a Start menu for launching applications and a windowed interface where multiple apps run simultaneously in resizable panels. Designers building for Windows can expect users to interact via mouse and keyboard, and to expect familiar navigation patterns such as right-click context menus.

Apple macOS runs exclusively on Apple’s own hardware. Its HCI uses a Dock at the bottom of the screen, a persistent menu bar at the top and a design language emphasised in Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines. macOS designers target a user base that expects visually polished, consistent interfaces with smooth animations. Software compatibility is narrower than Windows but the hardware and software ecosystem is tightly controlled.

Linux (and Ubuntu) is open-source and free. Ubuntu is a widely used distribution designed to be accessible to non-technical users. Linux HCIs vary significantly: some use graphical desktops resembling Windows; others are primarily command-line interfaces used by developers and system administrators. Because Linux can be configured so freely, HCI designers targeting Linux environments must account for a wide range of possible interface configurations.

Unix is the historical foundation from which both Linux and macOS evolved. Today it is found mainly in enterprise-grade server environments and academic institutions. Unix systems are typically operated via command-line interfaces, so they are not usually the target environment for consumer-facing HCI design — but the exam requires you to know it exists and its primary use context.

Chrome OS is Google’s lightweight operating system found on Chromebook devices, popular in schools. Its HCI is almost entirely browser-based: apps run in Chrome tabs rather than as locally installed programs. This has significant design implications — Chrome OS users expect web applications, and offline functionality is limited. Designers building for Chrome OS must prioritise responsive web design and cloud-based workflows.

Key Fact

The eight operating systems named in the specification are: Windows (business/education desktops), Apple macOS (Apple hardware), Apple iOS (iPhone/iPad), Android (most smartphones and tablets), Chrome OS (Chromebook laptops), Ubuntu (user-friendly Linux distribution), Linux (servers, developers), Unix (enterprise servers, academic systems).

Mobile Operating Systems

Apple iOS is a closed ecosystem — Apple controls exactly which apps can be installed, requiring all apps to go through the App Store and pass Apple’s review process. HCI design for iOS follows Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines closely: consistent navigation patterns, specific button sizes and placement conventions, and design expectations around gestures (swipe up to go home, long press for options). The closed ecosystem means fewer device variants to design for, but developers must follow Apple’s rules.

Android is open-source and used on devices from many different manufacturers. This makes it the most widely used mobile OS globally. However, it creates a design challenge: Android runs on devices with hugely varying screen sizes, processor speeds and display resolutions. A designer targeting Android must test across multiple device types and plan for responsive layouts that adapt to different dimensions. The Google Play Store distributes Android apps, but the approval process is less restrictive than Apple’s.

The OS creates the environment in which an HCI must operate — and each OS brings its own conventions, constraints and user expectations. On Windows, users expect right-click menus, resizable windows and keyboard shortcuts. On iOS, users expect swipe gestures, a consistent bottom navigation bar and no right-click functionality. On Linux, power users may prefer a command-line interface for speed and control. On Chrome OS, the interface must work primarily within a browser window.

Designing against the OS conventions produces poor HCI. An app that places navigation at the top of the screen on Android (where users expect it at the bottom) creates confusion. An interface that relies on hover effects will not work on any touch-based OS. Knowing the OS is therefore not optional in HCI design — it determines the interaction vocabulary the designer must use.

Digital Platforms

Operating systems run software — and the software environment the HCI is designed for is called the digital platform. The four digital platform types named in the specification are: database, mobile app, spreadsheet and website.

A database platform presents data in structured tables and forms. The HCI for a database typically includes search fields, data entry forms, filter controls and tabular displays. Users are often data professionals rather than general consumers. A mobile app is installed on a smartphone or tablet and uses the device’s touchscreen conventions. Its HCI must use large tap targets, limited navigation depth and mobile-specific interaction patterns. A spreadsheet platform (such as a desktop application or web-based tool) presents data in a grid of cells. HCI features include formula input, cell formatting and chart generation — designed for numeric analysis rather than casual browsing. A website runs in a browser and must be designed to work across different browsers, screen sizes and operating systems simultaneously. Responsive design — the ability to adapt the layout to different screen widths — is essential.

Exam questions on digital platforms often ask you to select and justify a platform for a scenario. Work through the user and task. A local GP surgery wanting to record patient appointment data with search and filter functionality → database (structured data, professional users). A national retailer wanting customers to browse and buy products on their phones → mobile app (touchscreen interaction, push notifications, stored payment details). A finance department needing to model budget forecasts → spreadsheet (formula-based calculations, chart output). A charity wanting to reach the widest possible audience with an information campaign → website (works on any device/OS without installation).

Key Fact

The four digital platforms are: database (structured data entry and retrieval, form-based HCI), mobile app (touchscreen interaction, large tap targets, installed on device), spreadsheet (grid-cell numerical data, formula input, charts), website (browser-based, responsive across devices and OS, no installation needed).
exam_tip_html: Operating system questions frequently use “explain” or “describe”. Naming an OS without linking it to HCI design impact scores only partial marks. Always connect the OS to the interaction patterns it creates: for example, “iOS uses a closed ecosystem, meaning designers must follow Apple’s guidelines, which requires consistent button placement and swipe gesture conventions throughout the app.” For digital platform questions, justify your choice by linking the platform’s characteristics to the specific user need in the scenario — avoid vague answers like “a website is easy to use.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The eight operating systems named in the specification are Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Chrome OS, Ubuntu, Linux and Unix — each has a primary use context and its own HCI conventions that designers must follow.
  • iOS is a closed ecosystem controlled by Apple; Android is open-source and runs across a wide range of device types. Both shape the interaction patterns, navigation conventions and design guidelines a developer must follow.
  • Digital platforms (database, mobile app, spreadsheet, website) determine the structure and style of the HCI — each platform is suited to different types of tasks and users, and exam questions require you to justify which platform fits a given scenario.

practice_questions.text: Which operating system runs on Chromebook laptops and delivers most of its functionality through a browser rather than locally installed applications?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Chrome OS (only). Distractors: Windows (uses locally installed applications), Ubuntu (Linux distribution, not browser-based by default), iOS (mobile OS, not found on laptops).

practice_questions.text: Identify one key difference between iOS and Android as mobile operating systems.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one accurate contrast, e.g. iOS is a closed ecosystem where all apps must be approved by Apple (1); OR Android is open-source and runs on devices from many different manufacturers, whereas iOS runs only on Apple devices (1); OR Android is used on a wider range of screen sizes and hardware specs, requiring designers to plan for more variation (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline how the operating system choice affects HCI design for a developer creating a productivity application.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: each OS has its own design conventions and interaction patterns (1); for example, Windows users expect resizable windows and keyboard shortcuts while iOS users expect swipe gestures and a specific bottom navigation bar, so the designer must follow the target OS conventions or the HCI will feel unfamiliar and be harder to use (1). Accept other valid OS-specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Describe the characteristics of a database as a digital platform, and explain why it suits a professional data entry context.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: a database platform presents data in structured tables and forms with search, filter and data entry controls (1); this suits professional data entry because users need to retrieve specific records quickly, enter validated data accurately and view multiple related fields simultaneously — tasks the database HCI is specifically designed to support (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the operating system affects the HCI design choices available to a developer creating an interface for Android compared with iOS.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies that Android is open-source and runs on devices from many manufacturers with varying screen sizes and hardware specifications (1); explains the HCI design consequence: the developer must create responsive layouts that adapt to different screen dimensions and cannot assume a consistent hardware baseline (1); contrasts with iOS: the closed ecosystem and strict Human Interface Guidelines constrain design choices but mean the developer can target fewer device variants with a more controlled visual standard (1).
Secure (2): OS difference stated and one clear HCI design consequence explained; second platform underdeveloped.
Developing (1): identifies that the two platforms differ without explaining specific HCI design implications.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Sketch a mapping of the eight operating systems to their primary device types and use contexts. For each OS, note one HCI design implication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): sketch or structured table identifies all eight OS entries (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Chrome OS, Ubuntu, Linux, Unix) with accurate primary device type and at least one HCI implication for each. Sample answers: Windows — business/education desktop, taskbar + Start menu conventions, mouse and keyboard input (1); macOS — Apple hardware only, Dock + menu bar, polished visual guidelines (1); iOS — iPhone/iPad, closed App Store, swipe gestures, consistent nav conventions (1); Android — multi-manufacturer smartphones, open-source, responsive layouts needed across device sizes (1); Chrome OS — Chromebook, browser-based apps, web-first responsive design (1); Ubuntu — user-friendly Linux on desktops, graphical desktop similar to Windows but highly configurable (1); Linux — servers/developer machines, command-line primary, minimal graphical HCI (1); Unix — enterprise/academic servers, command-line interface, rarely the target of consumer HCI (1).
Secure (5–6): six or seven OS entries with accurate types and implications.
Developing (3–4): four or five entries; some implications missing or inaccurate.
Emerging (1–2): fewer than four entries; implications largely absent.
0: no creditworthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: Which operating system is described as open-source and runs on devices from many different manufacturers?
Which digital platform uses a grid of cells, is designed for numerical analysis, and supports formula input and chart generation?
The operating system manages a device's hardware resources, runs software applications, and presents the _____ through which users interact with the device.
iOS is described as a _____ ecosystem because Apple controls which apps can be installed, requiring all applications to pass through the App Store.
Match each operating system to its primary use context.
right: Chromebook laptops — most functionality via browser

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three core jobs of an operating system?
flashcard_questions.a: Manage hardware resources, run software applications, present the HCI.

flashcard_questions.q: Which OS is found on Chromebook laptops and is almost entirely browser-based?
What makes iOS a closed ecosystem?
flashcard_questions.a: Apple controls app installation — all apps must be approved and distributed through the App Store.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Android create more HCI design challenges than iOS?
flashcard_questions.a: Android runs on many manufacturers' devices with varying screen sizes and specs, requiring responsive layouts.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four digital platform types in the specification.
Which digital platform is best for reaching the widest audience with no installation required?
flashcard_questions.a: Website — runs in any browser on any OS without installation.

flashcard_questions.q: What OS is the historical foundation for both Linux and macOS?
What HCI design convention does Windows use that shapes user expectations?
flashcard_questions.a: Taskbar at the bottom, Start menu, resizable windows, right-click context menus.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a Chrome OS app be designed around web-based functionality?
flashcard_questions.a: Chrome OS runs almost all apps through the Chrome browser — locally installed software is not the norm.
The software environment (database, app, spreadsheet, website) within which an HCI operates.

glossary_terms.definition: Software that manages a device's hardware resources, provides a platform for other software to run on, and presents the interface through which users interact with the device.
A family of desktop and laptop operating systems developed by Microsoft; the dominant OS in business and educational environments, known for its Start menu, taskbar and wide software compatibility.
Apple's desktop and laptop operating system; known for its Dock navigation bar, macOS-specific design guidelines and tight integration with Apple hardware.

An open-source family of operating systems built on the Linux kernel; freely available and widely used on servers, supercomputers and developer machines. Ubuntu is a popular user-friendly distribution.
One of the oldest operating systems, developed at Bell Labs; it forms the foundation for both Linux and macOS, and is used primarily in large-scale enterprise and academic server environments.

Google's lightweight operating system designed primarily for Chromebook laptops; almost all functionality runs through the Chrome browser and web-based applications rather than locally installed software.
Apple's mobile operating system for iPhone and iPad; a closed ecosystem where all apps must be approved by Apple and distributed through the App Store.
Google's open-source mobile operating system; used on the vast majority of smartphones and tablets from many different manufacturers.
The software environment or application type within which an HCI is designed to operate, such as a database, mobile app, spreadsheet or website.
